title: Gifts for a 5-Year-Old Who Loves Masking Tape and Crafts
h1_options: The tape won’t come off the roll
Tape, cardboard and a felt mask
h1: The tape won’t come off the roll
kicker_tail: for a boy turning five who builds with tape
sub: Gift ideas for an almost-five-year-old who builds things out of masking tape but can’t get it off the roll by himself. He also has Magna-Tiles, BRIO track and a teepee he likes to sit in, and when he isn’t in it he moves through the house like a luchador. Lately he has asked for face paint, his own nail polish and clothes, and those three sections follow the luchador things. Drew set the rules: under $75 each, nothing big, messy or loud, and it has to arrive by Christmas. The tape fixes come first, and the projector after them is a secondhand toy from 2003, chosen because the reels it plays are still sold by the boxful.
meta_description: Gift ideas for a boy turning five who builds with masking tape: tape he can tear, a used View-Master projector, Makedo kits and lucha masks.
picks_why: The tape center fixes the problem he has today, with eight rolls on a wooden stand and a plastic edge to cut against. The View-Master projector, a used toy from 2003, takes any View-Master reel; he drops one in and works the lever himself, and $20 of secondhand reels gives him more than a hundred pictures. The felt mask costs $16, fits a child’s face, and makes him a luchador by dinner.
box1h: It’s the hole in the roll
box1: Ordinary masking and painter’s tape is wound on a 3-inch core, and most desk dispensers take a 1-inch one, so a desk dispenser won’t hold the tape he uses. Classroom tape stations with a plastic cutting edge get around that, but most cost about $99, and Lakeshore’s half-inch station at $69.99 is the one under the ceiling. It runs on its own narrow tape. For $19, Uline’s three-roll dispenser takes the masking tape already in the house, behind a metal blade a grown-up has to mind, and narrow craft tape that tears by hand skips the dispenser altogether.
box2: Drew’s test had two parts: a five-year-old can run it alone, and the pictures are either homemade or in a standard format that turns up secondhand. View-Master reels pass the second half, and in the early 2000s Fisher-Price made battery projectors for children that pass the first. The instruction sheet for the 2003 Show & Tell model says to “Insert any View-Master reel into the slot near the projector lens.” On November 27 eBay had more than 4,000 lots of reels at roughly $1 to $1.50 a reel, seven pictures on each, so $20 buys fifteen to twenty. Reels can’t carry his own drawings, because the one company printing custom ones says they work only in its own viewer.
legend: Everything with a card was in stock and under $75 when we opened its listing in a browser on November 27, 2026. The used things, two projectors and the reels, link to an eBay search rather than one listing, and their prices are the range that search showed the same day. Prices and stock change, so expect some of this to have moved. Amazon wasn’t checked, because its pages bar AI agents.

tape.title: Tape he can run
tape.intro: The tape center fixes the dispenser problem, and the craft tape gets around it by tearing in his hands. The Uline dispenser is the one that takes the masking tape already in the house.

build.title: Cardboard and labels
build.intro: Makedo is the building he already does with tape, moved into cardboard boxes and held together with screws he can back out and use again. The label maker gives each build a name, and the paint sticks give it color.

proj.title: Projectors
proj.intro: The View-Master projector comes first, then the reels it plays and an older model that plays the same ones. The art projector puts his own drawings on the wall, and the photo flashlight holds one reel of the family’s photos.

cozy.title: In the teepee
cozy.intro: He already owns a Yoto, so four of these feed it: blank cards for stories the family records, two story cards and a case to keep them in. The rest is for the time he spends inside, with a sleeping bag, a weighted puppy for his lap and a weighted dog to carry, things to build or turn in his hands, and books and puzzles that need nobody else. The last two are a cloth mouse and a tent of its own, to set up inside his. No floor cushion under $75 could be confirmed to fit, so there isn’t one.

sets.title: Tiles and trains
sets.intro: Each of these changes what his Magna-Tiles or BRIO track can do. The train-track toppers are the only thing here that works with both.

lucha.title: Luchador
lucha.intro: A child-size lucha mask from a US seller was the hardest thing on this page to find. Most masks sold as youth sizes are cut for ages 6 to 12 or ship from abroad, and two Etsy shops had a kid size arriving in December. Last is a foam pogo jumper, for when the wrestling turns into jumping.

face.title: Face paint and tattoos
face.intro: Face paint comes in two kinds. Cakes need water, a brush and a grown-up to paint; sticks, crayons and pens need none of that, and he can use them himself in front of a mirror. We didn’t find a luchador tattoo sheet at a US shop, so half of the tattoo picks start from his own drawings, printed onto tattoo paper, drawn on his arm with skin pens or cranked into stickers. Wooly Willy puts a beard on a face with nothing to wash off.

nails.title: His own polish
nails.intro: Kids’ polish makes you choose. Piggy Paint dries hard and stays, which means a remover that is alcohol-based and for a grown-up to use; the Petite Manucurist and Nailmatic polishes come off with soap and water and don’t last. The pens let him do his own nails with no brush and no open bottle. The last two take the small brush somewhere else, onto a bare BRIO train, and then do without the brush entirely.

dress.title: A look of his own
dress.intro: The first cape is blank until he colors it, so what he wears starts as something he made. The others lean toward the ring: a luchador mask sewn onto green satin, and a gold lightning bolt fit for a wrestler’s entrance. We found no sequin cape in his size in stock at a US shop. Billy lets him put together a look on a wooden figure, and the three picture books are about people who made, or wanted, clothes of their own. The suitcase at the end holds clothes for the mouse from the teepee.

gear.title: Grown-up gear, small
gear.intro: Things an adult carries, made to fit him. Half of them light up.

wild.title: Unrelated, on purpose
wild.intro: Drew asked for ideas past anything he’d described. Each of these has a mechanism to work out, like a bird that flies on a rubber band or a top that turns itself over.

do.title: To do, not to own
do.intro: Two subscriptions that put something with his name on it in the mailbox, and a lucha show for a family willing to stay up.

cut.title: Checked and left out
cut.intro: These were priced or opened and didn’t make it, and each has its reason beside it. Drew read this page twice, and each reading took a few things off it. A couple were only sold out and may come back.

notes.tapecenter: He pulls a strip, tears it on the edge, and nobody has to start the roll for him. Refills have to be Lakeshore’s own half-inch tape.
notes.colorations: Tape that tears by hand needs no dispenser, so there is nothing to start and nothing to cut. The masking tape will look plain next to it.
notes.uline: An industrial dispenser that takes the rolls already in the house. The blade is metal, so the dispenser lives where a grown-up can see it.
notes.makedo-discover: This is where tape leads: cardboard he cuts himself, joined with screws he can back out and use again. Start saving boxes now.
notes.makedo-explore: A smaller box for finding out whether cardboard holds him the way tape does. The screws are just as small as the bigger kit’s.
notes.dymo: Each letter is a turn of the wheel and a firm squeeze, and out comes a raised label for his latest build. Reviews disagree on how long it lasts.
notes.kwikstix: He twists up a stick and colors his cardboard builds with it, so there is no pot of paint open on the table. The seller says it dries in under 90 seconds and needs no brush or water.
notes.vmprojector: It’s a used toy from about 2003, so ask the seller whether they tested it, and keep a spare bulb in mind. Take the reel out and it’s a flashlight.
notes.vmreels: This is the part he’ll go through. It’s a used lot, so ask for a photo of the titles, or he may get forty national parks and one cartoon.
notes.vmtelescope: The same reels play in it, which makes it the fallback if no Show & Tell turns up. It’s secondhand too, so ask whether the tripod comes with it.
notes.eztracer: The one way here to put his own drawings on the wall. A grown-up sets it up and plugs it in, and he hands over the pictures.
notes.photoflash: The reel of family photos is ordered after the box arrives, so wrap the flashlight and let the photos follow.
notes.yotomyo: Someone reads his favorite books aloud once, and the Yoto he already has plays them back as often as he asks.
notes.yotoconstruction: At five minutes a story, “one more” is an easy yes.
notes.yotothomas: For a boy with BRIO track, an hour of engines he doesn’t have to push.
notes.yotocase: Cards go missing in blankets, and this gives the teepee one place to keep them.
notes.sleepingbag: It turns the teepee into somewhere to sleep, at least until someone carries him to bed.
notes.lappad: Three pounds of stuffed puppy across his legs at the end of a loud day. It asks him to sit still without anyone saying so.
notes.weightedlab: The lap pad lies flat across his legs, and this is a weighted dog he can carry around and hold. It weighs two and a half pounds and costs about a third as much.
notes.camelot: Wooden blocks, a knight to get across them, and an hour in the teepee when he wants nobody else in there.
notes.patternblocks: A flat cousin of his Magna-Tiles: he copies a picture shape by shape, and a bump of the knee doesn’t undo it.
notes.prismcube: Something for his hands while a story plays, with no battery and nothing to put back together.
notes.forts: A picture book about forts, for a boy who reads in one.
notes.journey: Every page is a picture, so the story is whatever he says it is that night.
notes.dark: For the teepee after dark, read by whichever lamp he’s holding.
notes.stickers: The nearest thing here to tape: he sticks things down, peels them up and starts over, and nothing ends up on the furniture.
notes.glowpuzzle: He builds it with a light on, then switches it off to see the skeletons. Plan on doing the edges with him the first time.
notes.mouse: Someone smaller than he is to look after in the teepee: a cloth mouse in pajamas who gets put to bed in a matchbox, with a blanket and a pillow. There are magnets in both paws.
notes.mousetent: A tent for the mouse, set up inside the one he sits in. It has a padded floor and a small window, and wooden sticks hold the door open under the awning. The mouse comes separately.
notes.railracers: Clear rails clip onto tiles he already has and turn a tower into a ball run. The ball is small, so it goes on a shelf at night.
notes.toppers: The one thing on the page that joins his two sets, laying printed track across a tile floor. It’s clearance stock and may not last.
notes.builder: Two cranes that reach up and set tiles in place, which gives a tall build somewhere to go. Part of the box is more tiles.
notes.bridge: He cranks the span up, and every train on the line waits for him to let it down.
notes.turntable: Seven tracks meet at one spinning plate, so a single engine can be sent anywhere on the layout.
notes.crossing: The engine’s own magnet drops the barrier as it goes by. Expect it to be tested many times before anything else gets built.
notes.supports: Track high enough to build under, which means Magna-Tile tunnels and stations beneath the BRIO line.
notes.cars: Two magnetic chassis that put wheels under whatever he builds. It’s the cheapest way here to make the tiles move.
notes.downhill: Ramps and two wheeled riders, so a tower has a way down as well as up. Of the tile sets here it costs the most.
notes.mask-felt: Soft felt, cut for a child’s face, which most lucha masks we found were not. Of the luchador gifts, it has the least that can go wrong.
notes.mask-full: The full pullover look, from a California shop that makes a kid size. The listing has no size chart, so ask the seller for measurements first.
notes.mask-kit: He builds his own mask from sticky foam, so it’s a craft before it’s a costume. Twelve kits means eleven for friends or stuffed animals.
notes.belt: Something to win and defend in the living room. It’s WWE rather than lucha, and cut for six and up, so it may hang long on him.
notes.nino: The luchador picture book, and the obvious one for a boy who wrestles. Bookshop.org is out until February, so the link goes to Barnes & Noble.
notes.training: Comic panels let him follow the story before he can read it. A good one for the night after Niño.
notes.vamos: Same author as Training Day, with pages crowded enough that he’ll still be finding things after he knows the story.
notes.pogo: Somewhere for the jumping to go: he stands on the foam, holds the handles and jumps, indoors or out. A built-in squeaker sounds on every jump, which stretches the rule about nothing loud.
notes.headlamp: He has lights for the teepee already. This one goes where he looks, including into the cardboard fort the Makedo kit will sooner or later produce.
notes.safe: Two locks on a metal box, for whatever a five-year-old decides is valuable. Keep a spare key somewhere he doesn’t know about.
notes.watch: A reason to ask how long until dinner, and eventually a way to check the answer himself.
notes.binoculars: For birds in the yard and trucks down the street. The bag gives them somewhere to live besides the floor.
notes.flashlight: Clipped to a belt loop, it goes wherever he goes, which is most of what a flashlight is for.
notes.squeeze: It lights only while he squeezes, so it can’t be left burning under the bed.
notes.timbird: Wind the rubber band, let go, and it flaps off across the park. It’s fragile, so this is for open grass and a grown-up’s hands at first.
notes.musicbox: He punches holes in a paper strip, cranks it through, and hears the song he wrote. The punching takes help at first.
notes.labyrinth: Two knobs tilt the board to steer a steel ball past the holes. Expect him to lose to it for a long while.
notes.dragon: A board game short enough to finish before attention runs out. The gems are small and many, so play at the table and count them back in.
notes.rushhour: Slide the other vehicles around until his gets out of the jam. It’s a quiet thing to hand him when the wrestling needs a break.
notes.top: Spin it on its round end and partway through it flips over onto its stem. Explaining why can wait a few years.
notes.kamifusen: Paper cubes he blows up himself and bats around the house, too light to knock anything over. When they tear, you buy four more.
notes.beetle: Wind it and it crawls across the table with its wings going. It’s small enough to come out of a pocket at a restaurant.
notes.rainbow: On a sunny morning it sends rainbows sliding around his room with nobody touching it. Mount it high, where the crystal stays out of reach.
notes.rangerrick: A magazine addressed to him, which at five is half the gift. The first issue may come after Christmas, so wrap a printout of the order.
notes.kiwico: One building project a month, for a boy who already builds with tape. He’s near the top of the age range and will move up to Kiwi Crate soon.
notes.lucha-live: Masked wrestlers in person, if a tour date is within a drive. It means a late night in a loud arena, so plan it like a trip.
notes.facesticks: The cheapest way for him to paint his own face, standing at a mirror with no water and no grown-up holding a brush. Soap takes it off.
notes.luchapalette: Jest Paint sells it as a superhero kit, and its red, white and black are also the colors of a lucha mask. The cakes are full size, from a face painters’ supplier, and a grown-up holds the brush.
notes.snazadventure: The most colors of any kit here, with stick-on stencils and a step-by-step guide for whoever is painting. Each pot holds 2 ml, and the kit alone was $15.75 on sale.
notes.brushpens: Brush-tip pens that need no water, so he can draw his own outlines in black and white. The red, gold and blue pack was sold out.
notes.goldcrayon: Gold he can put on himself, for the trim of a mask. It makes the opposite trade from the Snazaroo sticks: it stays on through sweat and comes off only with makeup wipes.
notes.facebook: This one is for whoever is painting. He points at a tiger or a shark in the visual index, and it sends you to the page that shows how.
notes.tattoopens: He draws the tattoo himself, copying the guitars, stars and skulls on the cards or making up his own. Soap and water take it off, and tomorrow he can draw another.
notes.trucktats: The plain tattoo, since we didn’t find a luchador sheet at a US shop. Over fifty trucks, tires and trophies, each lasting up to five days.
notes.glowtats: Tattoos that glow in the dark, so he has something to check on his arm in the teepee with the light off.
notes.tattoopaper: This is how one of his drawings becomes a tattoo. A grown-up scans it, prints it on an inkjet and cuts it out, and it goes on with water. There are only two sheets, so pick the drawings first.
notes.rubons: The same press, rub and peel as a temporary tattoo, with the picture landing on a construction site, a racetrack or a city. He rubs with a pencil, and nothing goes on skin.
notes.stickermaker: He feeds in anything flat up to five inches wide, turns the knob, and it comes out a sticker. For a boy who builds with tape, it makes his drawings into something he can stick down.
notes.woolywilly: Face paint with nothing to wash off: he drags iron powder into sideburns and a moustache on a bald face with a magnet. It costs $3.99.
notes.polishpens: A marker tip lets him do his own nails with no brush and no open bottle. No black pen is made, so the luchador colors come in bottles.
notes.luchapolish: Black, gold glitter and matte red, the colors of a luchador, sold only as bottles. They dry hard and stay, so plan on the remover, which is alcohol-based and a grown-up’s job.
notes.boum: The wash-off kind: it peels off or comes off with soap and water, so a smudge costs nothing. It won’t last like Piggy Paint, and it’s final sale.
notes.manucurist: He picks the three colors, and soapy water takes them off, so no remover comes into the house. They won’t outlast a bath, which leaves him free to paint again the next night.
notes.glowpolish: Clear under the lamp and green in the dark, so the teepee is where he’ll go to look at his nails. It needs remover, like the other Piggy Paint bottles.
notes.tweexy: Made for grown-ups, it grips the table on a suction base and holds an open bottle where an elbow can’t tip it over.
notes.painttrain: Nail polish is careful color on a small surface with a small brush, and this is the same job on a bare BRIO engine and two cars. Once dry it runs on his track, and he can paint it again.
notes.fingerprint: Pictures made from a fingerprint and a few pen lines, so his fingertips do the painting. It needs a washable ink pad, which doesn’t come with the book.
notes.colorcape: He colors it in with the six markers in the box, so the cape is his design before he puts it on. Turned over, it’s red spider-print satin.
notes.luchacape: Handmade green satin with a blue felt luchador mask sewn on, where the wrestling and the clothes meet. Only two were left, and the shop takes no returns.
notes.wizardcape: Sold as a wizard’s cape, though a gold lightning bolt on black satin works as well for a wrestler walking out to the ring. It reverses to gold stars.
notes.shades: Matte black frames in the maker’s junior size, which starts at five. If he breaks them, Roshambo replaces them.
notes.billy: He swaps magnetic outfits on a wooden figure, from knight to firefighter, and puts together a look without a pile of clothes on the floor.
notes.patrickkelly: A picture-book life of the designer Patrick Kelly, who began as a boy at his grandmother’s table with a needle and thread. It treats clothes as something a person makes.
notes.julian: Julián sees three women dressed as mermaids on the subway and builds his own costume from a curtain and a potted fern.
notes.sparkleboy: Casey likes his blocks, puzzles and dump truck, and he also wants a shimmery skirt, glittery nails and a sparkly bracelet like his sister’s. It’s the one book here that touches both the polish and the clothes.
notes.mouseclothes: He has asked for clothes, and this time he dresses someone else. Green pants with orange suspenders and a polka-dot hat, sized for the Little Brother mouse, come packed in their own metal suitcase. The mouse is sold separately.

footer: A personal list, with no affiliate links and no paid placements. Every listing was checked on November 27, 2026.
